item.title: Topology-only Local Network Alignment, Part 2. DijSLA: Stochastic Greedy Extension for Cross-Species GO Annotation Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.26926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sequence similarity has long been a strong signal for protein function prediction, whereas the predictive value of network topology has been difficult to verify. Since a protein's function is largely defined by its interaction partners, and since similar interactions are expected across species, aligning protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks by topology alone should uncover functionally related proteins. Topology-only global network alignment has recently produced high-quality functional predictions, but it has yet to be shown that local regions of topological similarity can do the same. We introduce DijSLA (Dijkstra-inspired Stochastic Local Alignment), the first local network alignment algorithm designed from the ground up to use only topology. We adopt a seed-and-extend strategy: starting from seed pairs of proteins with similar network topology, we expand the alignment in a Dijkstra-inspired manner, following edges out of the aligned set to node pairs with near-maximal similarity. Rather than expanding deterministically, we inject randomness so that we can sample many high-quality alignments, in which node pairs with robust topological similarity "rise above" the noise and reveal functional similarity. Using networks and GO annotations from April 2010, we predict annotations validated against those from April 2020. With Network Alignment Frequency (NAF), a robustness measure that correlates with prediction precision, we make predictions with precision on par with or better than the best sequence-based methods and broadly similar to that of global topological alignment. Compared with existing local aligners, DijSLA produces larger, topologically high-quality alignments, which yield dramatically more predictions with higher validation rates, while using less CPU time and far less memory. Code is available at https://github.com/waynebhayes/BLANT/tree/master/CDijkstra.
item.dc:creator: Yiran Jin, Tingyin Ding, Utsav Jain, Grady Jaron Yu, Burwin Liu, Wayne B. Hayes

item.title: Mammalian gonadal development: origins, specification and differentiation of ovary and testis cell lineages
item.description: arXiv:2611.27933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Testicular and ovarian development requires the coordinated formation and assembly of multiple cell types that enable these organs to fulfill their roles in sexual differentiation, reproduction, and endocrine function. A defining feature of gonadal development is that both testes and ovaries arise from a common bipotential primordium, the genital ridge, composed of multipotent progenitors. In this Review, we synthesize current knowledge on the origin, specification, differentiation, and function of the major fetal gonadal somatic lineages, drawing primarily on mouse and human studies. We describe how the adrenogonadal primordium (AGP) gives rise to the gonadal primordium (GP), how coelomic epithelium-derived progenitors generate the supporting, steroidogenic/stromal, and supporting-like cell lineages, and how these progenitors become progressively fate-restricted. We highlight recent evidence for early lineage priming within spatially organized domains of the coelomic epithelium. We further examine the molecular pathways and cellular processes governing sex-specific differentiation of these lineages and discuss remaining gaps in our understanding of how bipotential gonads differentiate into testes or ovaries, and their implication for human health.
item.dc:creator: Serge Nef, Maeva Guy, Marie-Christine Chaboissier

item.title: An Open Petri Net Implementation of Gene Regulatory Networks
item.description: arXiv:1907.11316v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are a central object of systems biology, and many formalisms have been used to model them, among them Petri nets. Ordinary Petri nets, however, provide no built-in way to assemble a large network from smaller, separately specified pieces. Open Petri nets, in the sense of Baez and Master, supply exactly this: an open Petri net is a Petri net with designated boundary places, and open Petri nets are composed by gluing boundaries together (a pushout), giving a symmetric monoidal double category Open(Petri). In this paper we (i) state precisely the standard encoding of activation, inhibition and degradation as Petri net transitions; (ii) distinguish the classical "Petri nets are monoids" view of Meseguer and Montanari, which describes how processes inside one net compose, from the open Petri net view, which describes how nets compose; (iii) show, with a worked example, how a GRN can be cut into open Petri net modules along shared genes and recovered exactly by composition, together with simple rules that make such a decomposition correct; and (iv) use the compositional rate-equation semantics of Baez and Pollard to show that the mass-action dynamics of the composite network are obtained by gluing the dynamics of its modules, linking Petri net models of GRNs to their ordinary differential equation counterparts. We close by discussing what the reachability semantics does and does not give for GRN modules, and the limitations of the approach.
